title: Driven Quantum Stars as Controlled Primitives for Real-Time Spin Dynamics
abstract: Quantum advantage in real-time spin dynamics should be assessed against the strongest relevant classical substitutes, not merely against the qubit nature of the microscopic system. We develop a physics-based diagnostic for this boundary by reducing a qubit spin model to a spin-Landau--Lifshitz (LL) classical sector and organizing the residual quantum sector as controlled corrections. The control parameter is graph coordination: we study a spin star with \(d\) leaves and \(O(1/d)\) hub--leaf couplings. In its homogeneous form the star benchmarks the transition from LL-substitutable dynamics to genuinely quantum, discrete-sector interference; in its fully driven form, with time-dependent fields and bilinear couplings, it is the basic message-passing primitive for tree and loopy spin structures. For coherent-state return amplitudes we prove exact leaf elimination and derive a continuous-time \(1/d\) hierarchy. L0 is a driven one-spin weak-mean-field theory, while G1 is a Gaussian nonlocal-in-time influence correction coupling leaf two-time kernels to the hub weak two-point function. On bounded finite-time windows away from zeros of the boundary amplitudes, the hierarchy gives \(\log\mathcal A-\log\mathcal A_{\rm L0}=O(1/d)\) and \(\log\mathcal A-\log\mathcal A_{\rm L0}-Δ_{\rm G1}=O(1/d^2)\); numerical tests on fully driven anisotropic ensembles give slopes \(-1.05\) and \(-2.03\). Static, inhomogeneous, aligned, and fully driven stars provide validation rungs, and comparison with a temporal matrix-product influence-matrix baseline delineates complementary regimes. Unlike rank compression on a Trotter grid, the hierarchy is ordered by a physical parameter, formulated in continuous time, and each truncation level is itself a physical theory, with the LL sector as the high-coordination limit.
summary: The paper introduces a novel theoretical framework to diagnose quantum advantage in real-time spin dynamics by analyzing 'quantum star' graphs. It develops an approximation hierarchy, expanding the full qubit model around a classical Landau–Lifshitz sector using graph coordination ($1/d$) as the expansion parameter. This method provides quantitative bounds on when genuine quantum interference effects become essential for describing system evolution.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a rigorous diagnostic tool to determine when real-time quantum spin dynamics can be accurately approximated by classical models, such as the Landau–Lifshitz equation.
main_result: The authors developed an expansion hierarchy based on graph coordination ($1/d$) that systematically quantifies the deviation from classical behavior, showing that quantum corrections are necessary for accurate long-time predictions.
method: They employ a systematic approximation hierarchy by performing exact leaf elimination on a 'quantum star' graph structure. This allows them to derive continuous-time expansions in terms of weak mean-field theories ($L_0$) and Gaussian influence corrections ($G_1$).
model_or_system: The system is a driven quantum spin star composed of one hub and $d$ leaves, modeled by a time-dependent Hamiltonian. The analysis focuses on the coherent-state return amplitude as the primary observable.
key_observables: Coherent-state return amplitude ($A(T)$), $\log A - \log L_0$, and $\log A - \log L_0 - \Delta G_1$.
important_parameters: Graph coordination parameter $d$ (or $1/d$), time $T$, and the ratio of quantum correction to classical approximation.
main_assumptions: The analysis uses a single forward time contour for technical simplicity, although physical observables often require the full Keldysh closed-time-path contour. The hierarchy is ordered by the physical parameter $1/d$.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the diagnostic comparison between exact amplitude and approximations ($L_0$ vs $L_0+G_1$), showing $G_1$'s extension of validity. Figure 2 shows leaf elimination converting leaves into weak mean trajectories and two-time kernels acting on the hub.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the quantum star as a fundamental primitive, derives an exact leaf-elimination lemma, constructs a systematic expansion hierarchy ($L_0 	o G_1$), and validates this framework by comparing it against established methods like temporal matrix-product influence-matrix baselines.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, physically motivated diagnostic tool for quantum advantage in dynamics. For AMO/open systems researchers, the systematic $1/d$ expansion offers a controlled way to quantify when mean-field or classical approximations break down due to entanglement effects.

Figure 2: The driven star is the algorithmic primitive. Leaf elimination converts d quantum leaves into a weak mean trajectory and a two-time influence kernel acting on the hub. On larger trees the same object becomes a directed message from a subtree to its parent.

Fig. 2 also fixes the notation used below for the algorithmic interpretation: after elimination, a leaf or subtree contributes a scalar factor, a weak mean trajectory, and a two-time connected kernel. Throughout the paper, elimination means the exact contraction of the leaf world lines out of the amplitude (1): a quantum sum over the histories of the eliminated spins, conditioned on their coherent boundary data. It is the single-contour, fixed-boundary analogue of marginaliza- tion, performed at the amplitude level rather than at the density-matrix level – no partial trace is involved. (II) Leaf elimination (Lemma 1) is exact and produces continuum weak objects per leaf – a scalar, a weak mean trajectory, and a connected two-time kernel; the time grid enters only as a quadrature choice at numerical evaluation.
